results.title: Power, Effect Sizes, and Minimum Detectable Effects
results.content: # Power, Effect Sizes, and Minimum Detectable Effects. Power is sometimes also called “sensitivity.” Power refers to the ability of a test (i.e., an analysis of an experiment) to detect a “true effect” that is different from the null hypothesis (e.g., the ability to detect a difference between treatment and control when that difference actually exists). There are four factors that influence power: sample size, the true effect size, the variance of the effect, and the alpha-threshold (level of significance). If we have a more liberal threshold (i.e., a higher alpha level), we have more power to detect the effect. ## Power of a t-test. MDE tell us what is the smallest true effect, in standard deviations of the outcome, that is detectable for a given level of power and statistical significance. Because the standard deviation is influenced by sample size, MDE incorporates all of the information of a power calculation but does so in a way that applies to all experiments.

results.title: What is minimal detectable effect? How it impacts experiment results
results.content: MDE helps you understand the smallest effect size that your experiment is statistically powered to detect. Simply put, MDE is the smallest change in a metric that your experiment can detect with statistical significance. If you set a lower MDE to detect tiny changes, you'll need a larger sample size. Tools like Statsig's power analysis calculator can help you set the right MDE and plan your experiments efficiently. Remember, setting a lower MDE (to detect smaller changes) requires a larger **sample size**. By understanding how MDE impacts your sample size and leveraging the right tools, you can design experiments that are both effective and efficient. Understanding and carefully setting your Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) is key to running effective experiments. Tools like Statsig's power analysis calculator make it easier to plan and execute your experiments. If you're interested in learning more about experiment design and MDE, check out our resources at Statsig.

results.title: Power, minimal detectable effect, and bucket size estimation in A/B tests
results.content: They tend to either explicitly ask the experimenter the sample mean and standard deviation (in addition to overall population size) or they address “click through rate” (CTR) or “conversion” — binary-valued metrics (either 1 or 0) for which variance is easy to calculate given the ratio of 1s to 0s. Low statistical power means we can miss a positive change and dismiss an experiment that would have made a difference. If we use the convention of requiring power to be at least 80%, and make the simplifying assumptions that we have equal bucket sizes (n = m) and that the sigmas are the same, we can derive a nice formula for sample size n, as a function of true effect size and variance (via Kohavi et al [1]). Considering the high MDE, instead of concluding that the proposed improvement has no effect, it’s better to increase the sample size and re-run the experiment with higher power.
